en: The Śvetāśvatara-Upaniṣad (Śvetāśvataropaniṣad). Om. The Proponents of Brahman speak. Chapter One.
"What is the cause of Brahman? From where have we been born? By what do we live? And upon what are we established?
Governed by whom, O knowers of Brahman, do we abide in this arrangement amidst pleasure and its opposite? (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.1)
Time, inherent nature, necessity, chance, the elements, the womb, and the person—these are to be considered;
it is the conjunction of these [that produces the world], and not from the self's own being, for the self is indeed not the master over the cause of pleasure and pain. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.2)

Following the yoga of meditation, they beheld the divine power of the Self, concealed by its own qualities—that One who alone presides over all those causes joined with Time and the Self. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.3)

That [wheel] has one felly, is threefold, has sixteen ends, and fifty spokes; it has twenty counter-spokes, six sets of eight, a single rope of manifold forms, a division of three paths, two causes, and a single delusion. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.4)
We meditate upon that [Great River] which has five currents of water, five wombs as its fierce mouths, five vital breaths as its waves, and the five organs of perception as its source;
it has five whirlpools, the force of the flood of the fivefold miseries, fifty divisions, and five joints. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.5)
In that vast wheel of Brahman, which is the source of all livelihoods and the support of all things, the *haṃsa* (the individual soul) revolves.
Having perceived the Self as distinct from the impeller, and being thus favored by Him, one attains immortality. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.6)
This supreme Brahman is indeed sung as the Udgītha; within it are the three, the Self-established, and the Imperishable.
Having realized the distinction between these, those who know Brahman, being devoted to it, merge into Brahman and are liberated from the womb.
The Lord sustains this entire universe—the perishable and the imperishable, the manifest and the unmanifest—joined together.
Yet the self, though not the Lord, is bound by its state as an enjoyer; by knowing the God, one is released from all fetters. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.8)
The two unborn ones—the knowing and the ignorant—are the Lord and the non-Lord; for there is one unborn female (Prakṛti) joined with the enjoyer and the objects of enjoyment.
And the infinite Self is of universal form and is indeed a non-doer. When one perceives these three as this Brahman, [one attains liberation]. ŚvetU 1.9.
The perishable is the primary matter (pradhāna), and the imperishable is Hara; the one God rules over both the perishable and the self.

Through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through the realization of His true nature, there occurs at the end the cessation of the entire illusion of the world. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.10)
Having known the God, there is the falling away of all bonds; with the afflictions destroyed, there is the abandonment of birth and death.
Through meditation upon Him, upon the dissolution of the body, one attains absolute sovereignty over all things, being solitary and having all desires fulfilled. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.11)
This is to be known as eternally established in the Self; indeed, there is nothing further to be known beyond this.
Having understood the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller—all this has been declared as the threefold Brahman. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.12)
Just as the form of fire, when it has entered its source, is not seen, yet there is no destruction of its characteristic mark,
and it is again grasped from the source of its fuel— so indeed are both [the Self and the body] perceived within the body by means of the *praṇava*.
Making one's own body the lower fire-drill and the *praṇava* the upper fire-drill, through the practice of churning with meditation, one may behold the God as if hidden. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.14)

As oil in sesame seeds, as butter in curds, as water in flowing streams, and as fire in the fire-sticks—so is that Self grasped within the self by one who perceives it through truth and austerity. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.15)

The Self, all-pervading, like clarified butter contained in milk, has its root in the knowledge of the Self and austerity; that is Brahman, the supreme Upaniṣad—that is Brahman, the supreme Upaniṣad. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.16)
The Second Chapter:
Savitṛ, first yoking his mind and directing his thoughts toward the essential reality, having perceived the light of Agni, brought it forth from the earth. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.1)
With a disciplined mind, we [meditate] during the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the power for attaining the heavenly world. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.2)
Having yoked the gods with the mind, as they proceed toward heaven with their thought, Savitṛ impels those who are about to produce the great light from the sky. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.3)

The inspired poets harness their minds and they harness their thoughts for the sake of the great, inspired, wise one. He alone, knowing the sacred ordinances, ordains the priestly functions; great indeed is the praise of the god Savitṛ. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.4)
I yoke for you both an ancient prayer with prostrations; let the hymn go forth like a path toward the patron.
All the sons of immortality listen—those who have taken up their celestial abodes. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.5)
Where fire is churned forth, where the wind is obstructed, and where the soma-juice overflows—there the mind is born. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.6)
May he enjoy the ancient sacred word (brahman) through the impulse of Savitṛ; there you shall prepare a womb for yourself, for your gift has not been overlooked. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.7)

Holding the body straight with the three parts elevated, having withdrawn the senses into the heart by means of the mind, the wise one should cross over all perilous currents by means of the raft of Brahman. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.8)
Having restrained his vital breaths here through disciplined effort, he should breathe through the nostrils when the breath is exhausted;
like a chariot yoked to vicious horses, the wise man, remaining vigilant, should steady his mind. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.9)
In a clean place, free from pebbles, fire, and sand, and devoid of noise, water, and similar disturbances;
in a spot agreeable to the mind but not distressing to the eyes, one should practice in a cave or a sheltered place protected from the wind. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.10)
Frost, smoke, the sun, fire, wind, fireflies, lightning, crystal, and the moon—these are the preliminary forms that manifest Brahman in yoga. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.11)

When the fivefold quality of yoga, arising from earth, water, fire, air, and ether, has been set in motion, for him who has attained a body composed of the fire of yoga, there is no disease, no old age, and no death. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.12)

Lightness of body, health, freedom from greed, clarity of complexion, excellence of voice, a pleasant odor, and scantiness of urine and feces—they say these are the first signs of the onset of yoga. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.13)

Just as a statue coated with clay shines forth when it is well-burnished and filled with light, so too, having clearly perceived that reality of the Self, the embodied soul becomes solitary, fulfilled, and free from sorrow. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.14)

But when one endowed with yoga perceives here the reality of Brahman through the reality of the Self—likened to a lamp—knowing that God to be unborn, eternal, and purified by all principles, he is released from all fetters. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.15)
This God indeed pervades all the quarters; he was born first, and he is within the womb.
He alone has been born, and he is yet to be born; facing every direction, he stands before all people with faces on every side. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.16)

The god who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who has entered the entire world, who is in the plants, and who is in the trees—to that god, salutation after salutation! (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.17)
The Third Chapter.
He who alone, possessing a net, rules by his ruling powers, rules all worlds by his ruling powers;
he who alone exists at both emergence and dissolution—those who know this become immortal. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.1)
For Rudra is one; he does not stand for a second, he who rules these worlds by his ruling powers.
Facing all people, he stands; at the time of the end, having withdrawn all worlds, he, the guardian, contracts [himself]. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.2)

With eyes on every side and a face on every side, with arms on every side and feet on every side, the one God, generating heaven and earth, fans them together with his arms and wings. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.3)

May He who is the source and origin of the gods, the sovereign of all, Rudra the great seer, who in the beginning generated Hiraṇyagarbha—may He endow us with auspicious understanding. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.4)
O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is not terrible and does not reveal evil—with that most peaceful form, O Lord of the Mountain, look upon us with favor. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.5)
O Lord of the Mountain, that arrow which you carry in your hand to discharge—O Protector of the Mountain, make it auspicious; do not harm the person or the world. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.6)

Beyond that, having known Him—the Supreme Brahman, the Great One, hidden in all beings according to their respective forms, the one who envelops the universe, the Lord—they become immortal. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.7)
I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond the darkness. Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8)
Than whom there is nothing higher, than whom there is nothing smaller or greater;
like a tree, He stands alone, steadfast in heaven; by that Puruṣa all this is filled. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.9)
Then, that which is higher than this, formless and free from ailment—those who know this become immortal, while others enter only into suffering. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.10)
Having all faces, heads, and necks, dwelling in the secret cave of all beings, that Blessed One is all-pervading; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.11)
The Great Lord is indeed the Puruṣa; he is the instigator of this being (sattva).
He is the sovereign, the imperishable light, who has attained this utterly stainless state. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.12)

A person the size of a thumb is the inner self, eternally seated in the hearts of all people. He is fashioned by the heart, by intuition, and by the mind; those who know this become immortal. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.13)
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
Having pervaded the earth on every side, he stands beyond it by the measure of ten fingers. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.14)
The Person alone is all this—whatever has been and whatever is to be; moreover, he is the lord of immortality, that which grows by means of food. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.15)
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, and with ears everywhere in the world, it stands pervading all. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.16)
Manifesting the qualities of all the senses, yet devoid of all senses;
the Lord and Ruler of all, the refuge and friend of all. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.17)
In the city of nine gates, the embodied soul, like a swan, moves about outside;
it is the controller of the entire world, both the stationary and the moving. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.18)
Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper; he sees without eyes and hears without ears.
He knows that which is to be known, yet there is no knower of him. Him they call the foremost, the Great Person (mahān puruṣaḥ). (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19)
Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being;
freed from sorrow, he beholds that Lord of majesty, devoid of volition, through the clarity of the elements. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.20)
I know this undecaying, ancient one, the Self of all, who is omnipresent because of his pervasiveness;
for the exponents of Brahman indeed proclaim him eternally as the cessation of birth. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.21)
The Fourth Chapter:

He who, being one and colorless, through the application of his power, ordains many colors with a hidden purpose; who at the end withdraws the universe and at the beginning sends it forth—he is that God; may he endow us with auspicious intelligence. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.1)
That indeed is Agni, that is Āditya, that is Vāyu, and that is Candramas;
that indeed is Śukra, that is Brahman, that is the Waters, and that is Prajāpati. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.2)
You are woman; you are man; you are the youth, or even the maiden; you, as an old man, totter along with a staff; you are born, facing every direction. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.3)
Blue is the winged one, green, red-eyed; he contains lightning within him; he is the seasons and the oceans.
You are without beginning, existing through your omnipresence, from whom all the worlds have been born. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.4)
There is one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form;
one unborn male, rejoicing in her, lies by her, while another unborn male leaves her after he has enjoyed her pleasures. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5)
Two birds, inseparable companions and friends, nestle upon the same tree.
One of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.6)
On the same tree, a person is immersed and grieves, deluded by a sense of powerlessness;
but when he perceives the other as the beloved Lord and His majesty, he is freed from sorrow. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.7)

In the imperishable syllable within the supreme firmament, upon which all the gods are seated—what will he do with the Rigveda who does not know that? But those who know it, they sit here together in assembly. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.8)

The Vedas, sacrifices, rituals, and vows; the past, the future, and whatever the Vedas declare—the Magician creates all this, and another, distinct from him, is bound within it by his magic power. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.9)
One should know Māyā as Prakṛti (primordial matter) and Maheśvara as the wielder of Māyā;
by his constituent parts, this entire world is pervaded. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10)

He who alone presides over every womb, in whom this entire universe comes together and dissolves—having perceived that Lord, the boon-bestowing God worthy of praise, one attains this ultimate peace. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.11)
May Rudra, the great seer who is superior to all, the source and origin of the gods, beholding Hiraṇyagarbha as he is being born, endow us with auspicious understanding. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.12)

He who is the sovereign lord of the gods, upon whom the worlds are supported, who rules over these bipeds and quadrupeds—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.13)

Having known Him who is subtler than the subtlest, the creator of the manifold world in its midst, the one who encompasses the universe—having known that auspicious One, one attains ultimate peace. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.14)
He alone is the protector of the world at all times, the sovereign of all, hidden within all beings;
he to whom the Brahman-sages and the deities are united—knowing him thus, one cuts the bonds of death. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.15)

Having known Śiva, who is subtler than the cream on top of clarified butter, hidden within all beings, and having known the God as the one who envelops the universe, one is released from all bonds. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.16)
This divine Viśvakarman, the Great Self, is eternally seated within the hearts of all people;
fashioned by the heart, by insight, and by the mind—those who know this become immortal. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.17)
When there was darkness, that was neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being; Śiva alone existed.
That is the Imperishable, that is the most excellent glory of Savitṛ, and from it the ancient wisdom has issued forth. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.18)
Neither above, nor across, nor in the middle can anyone grasp him; there is no likeness of him whose name is Great Glory. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.19)
His form does not stand within the range of vision; no one sees him with the eye.
Those who know him thus as dwelling in the heart by means of the heart and the mind, they become immortal. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.20)
"Unborn"—thus does a certain fearful person take refuge.
O Rudra, with that face which is to the south, protect me forever. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.21)
Do not harm us in our children or grandchildren, nor in our life-span; do not harm us in our cattle or our horses.
O Rudra, do not slay our heroes in your wrath. Bearing oblations, we invoke you forever. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.22)

The Fifth Chapter: Two syllables, supreme to Brahman and infinite, are deposited therein, hidden—knowledge and ignorance. Ignorance is indeed the perishable, while knowledge is the immortal. He who rules over both knowledge and ignorance is another. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.1)
He who, being one, presides over every womb, over all forms and all wombs;
he who in the beginning supports with his knowledges the seer Kapila when he is born, and beholds him as he is being born. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.2)
Transforming each individual net manifoldly, this God withdraws it into this field;
having created it again, the Lord, the Great-Souled One, likewise exercises supreme sovereignty over all. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.3)
Just as the sun shines, illuminating all directions—above, below, and across—so does that one, exalted, adorable Lord, preside over the natures of the sources of being. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.4)
He who, as the source of the universe, ripens his own nature and transforms all things that are to be ripened;
he alone presides over this entire universe and ordains the application of all the qualities. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.5)
That which is hidden in the secret Upaniṣads of the Vedas—Brahmā knows that as the source of Brahman.
Those gods and seers of old who knew it became one with it and indeed attained immortality. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.6)

He who is associated with the qualities (guṇas), who performs actions for the sake of their fruits, and who is the enjoyer of what has been done—he, assuming all forms, consisting of the three qualities, following the three paths, and being the lord of the vital breaths, wanders about according to his own deeds. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.7)
The one who is the size of a thumb, whose form is like the sun, and who is endowed with volition and egoism;
by means of the quality of the intellect and the quality of the self, he is indeed seen as even smaller than the tip of an awl. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.8)
The individual soul (jīva) should be known as a part of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, divided again into a hundred parts; yet it is capable of infinity. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.9)
This is neither female nor male, nor indeed is it neuter;
whatever body it assumes, by that it is joined.
Through delusions of will, touch, and sight, and by means of food and rain, the embodied soul undergoes birth and growth;
following its past actions, it successively assumes various forms in different states of existence. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.11)
The embodied soul assumes many forms, both gross and subtle, through its own qualities;
moreover, another cause for their conjunction is observed, consisting of the qualities of action and the qualities of the self. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.12)

Having known the God who is without beginning or end, who dwells in the midst of the chaotic mass, the creator of the universe, possessing manifold forms, and the one sole enfolder of the universe—one is released from all fetters. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.13)

Those who know the God—who is to be grasped through contemplation, who is called the "nestless," who brings about both existence and non-existence, who is auspicious, and who effects the creation of the Kalās—have abandoned the body. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.14)
The Sixth Chapter:
Some poets speak of inherent nature (*svabhāva*), while others, being utterly deluded, speak of time (*kāla*).
But this is the majesty of the Divine in the world, by which this wheel of Brahman (*brahmacakra*) is made to revolve. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.1)
By Him indeed all this is ever pervaded—He who is the Knower, the Ordainer of Time, the possessor of qualities, and the All-Knowing.
Impelled by Him, the activity consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and ether revolves; thus it should be contemplated. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.2)
Having performed that action and turned away from it once more, having attained union with reality through reality itself—
whether by means of one, two, three, or eight factors, as well as time and the subtle qualities of the self— ŚvetU 6.3.

He who initiates actions endowed with qualities and employs all states of being—when those [actions and states] cease, his performed karma perishes; at the exhaustion of karma, he passes away to that which is truly other. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.4)

Having first worshipped that God who is the beginning, the cause of the motive for conjunction, who is seen as beyond the three times though himself timeless, who is the universal form, the source of existence, and worthy of praise, and who abides within one's own mind; ŚvetU 6.5.
He is the Supreme, other than whom this phenomenal world revolves through the forms of trees, time, and shapes;
having known Him—the bringer of dharma, the dispeller of evil, the Lord of Fortune, the immortal, the abode of all—residing within the self. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.6)
Let us know that God, the Lord of the world, worthy of praise—the supreme Maheśvara among lords, the supreme divinity among deities, and the highest lord beyond all lords. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.7)
For him there exists neither effect nor instrument; neither one equal to him nor superior to him is seen.
His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, and his knowledge, strength, and action are inherent. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8)
He has no master in the world, nor any ruler, nor indeed any mark; He is the cause, the lord of lords of the senses, and there is no progenitor of Him, nor any overlord.
May that one God, who by his own nature veils himself with the products of *pradhāna* as a spider does with its threads, grant us absorption into Brahman. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.10)
The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings;
He is the supervisor of actions, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, absolute and devoid of qualities. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11)

The one controller of the many inactive ones, who makes the single seed manifold—those wise ones who perceive Him abiding within themselves attain eternal happiness, and no others. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.12)

The eternal among the eternals, the consciousness among the conscious, the one who ordains the desires of many—having known that God, the cause which is to be attained through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, one is released from all fetters. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.13)

There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this earthly fire. Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.14)
There is but one swan in the midst of this world; he alone is the fire established within the waters.
Knowing him alone, one goes beyond death; there is no other path for the journey. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.15)
He is the maker of all, the knower of all, whose source is the Self; he is the conscious one, the ordainer of time, possessed of qualities, and the knower of all sciences.
He is the Lord of both Pradhāna and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), the Master of the Guṇas, and the cause of the bondage, maintenance, and liberation from saṃsāra. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.16)

Consisting of that, immortal, established in the Lord, the knower, all-pervading, the protector of this world—he alone rules over this universe eternally; no other cause exists for his lordship. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.17)
I, seeking liberation, take refuge in that God who created Brahmā in the beginning and who indeed imparts the Vedas to him—He who is the light of self-knowledge. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.18)
Partless, actionless, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless;
the supreme bridge to immortality, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19)
When men shall roll up space like a piece of leather, then, failing to recognize the Divine, there will be an end to suffering. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.20)

Then the wise Śvetāśvatara, through the power of austerity and by the grace of the gods, fully proclaimed this supreme purifier, which is cherished by the assembly of seers, to those who have transcended the stages of life. *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 6.21.
This supreme secret, taught in the Vedānta, was proclaimed in a former age;
it must not be given to one who is not tranquil, nor again to one who is not a son or a disciple. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.22)

For that great-souled one who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and for the teacher as for the Divine, these truths that have been declared indeed shine forth; they shine forth for the great-souled one. Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23.
